title: One ordering for configuration sources, and what a discovered file may not decide
summary: Every non-secret setting resolves in one order: explicit value for this run, user settings, composition, the launching shell's environment, discovered .env files, then defaults. A discovered .env file may not set sensitive names such as PATH.
firstReason: One precedence order with a known origin for each value is what makes a configured value explainable; keep it in the Go configuration loader.

title: Consumer-owned startup strictness
summary: The application, not the plugin framework, decides which components are required: boot checks a fixed list of entry ids after start-up and fails if a listed, enabled entry is not active; any other inactive entry is only a warning.
firstReason: Best-effort loading with an explicit required list is the right policy for the Go loader too; the list itself changes because the client module entries no longer exist.

title: Add immutable profile resolution generations
summary: Profile start-up computes one immutable answer to which npm package each name resolves to and installs it into Node's module resolvers; a change publishes a complete successor in one step, with no symlinks or generated proxy packages on disk.
firstReason: Node module resolution does not exist in Go. The goal (one atomic, immutable description of the plugin set for a process) is met by the compiled-in component registry plus an immutable manifest of plugin processes.

title: Current-profile plugin management shares CLI transactions
summary: The web plugin manager and the dsh plugin command call the same package operations under one profile lock, and hot reload applies module, include and profile changes through one queue so that a half-written manifest is never loaded.
firstReason: Shared operations under one writer lock are kept, but installing a plugin no longer runs pnpm and applying it no longer hot-swaps modules: the host starts, restarts or stops plugin processes.

title: Guided plugin installation
summary: The host inspects an install request before running it and reports one of seven specific problems; a failed or cancelled installation restores the profile's files.
firstReason: Inspecting before installing and rolling back on failure are kept, applied to plugin process packages instead of pnpm and package.json.

title: Creator mode installs persistent plugin bundles
summary: The agent can install a plugin bundle (a package plus a config patch) mid-conversation through the existing `plugin_manager` tool, in the Creator and Standard presets. Every call needs the full-access sandbox mode or a one-call approval, because a profile change can load code with host permissions and affects other sessions.
firstReason: The goal stands: an agent adds a capability and uses it in the same conversation, behind an explicit approval. In Go a bundle cannot be an npm package loaded into the host; it is a plugin process or an MCP configuration entry, so the install path and the risk being approved both change.

title: Plugin install registries
summary: Plugin installs ask an ordered plan of npm registries (the configured one, then mirrors such as npmmirror), so installs work where registry.npmjs.org is unreachable. A private registry is always asked alone and never falls back to a public one.
firstReason: The mechanism is pnpm and npm registries, which do not exist in Go. Two goals carry to whatever source the Go design downloads plugin processes from: a configurable mirror for networks that cannot reach the default, and no fallback from a private source to a public one (a same-named public package would be someone else's code).

title: Resolve profile modules along the ancestor chain with an interception layer
summary: Defines how Node resolves a module imported from inside a profile: Node's normal ancestor `node_modules` search, plus one interception that maps declared peer dependencies of linked packages to the host's runtime copy.
firstReason: Exists only because of Node module resolution and the npm package layout. Go components are linked at build time and plugin processes share no modules with the host (DH-ADR-4), so there is no lookup order to define.

title: Fatal diagnostics and Desktop crash reports
summary: An uncaught error is fatal: the host writes one full diagnostic, runs its release hook under a timeout and exits, never resuming the failed operation. Output spill files are best-effort, the desktop app writes a crash-report file before showing its fatal dialog, and a client script batch that failed in transport is retried once but never re-executed.
firstReason: Only the failing code knows which state is still valid, so continuing turns a visible crash into silently wrong output. Go's default for a panic in a goroutine is already to exit; the design must add the full diagnostic, the bounded release and the crash-report file. The client batch-retry part has no counterpart (DH-ADR-3).

title: Refresh runtime resolution after package operations and expire HMR package configuration
summary: After a plugin package is installed, enabled, disabled or removed while the host runs, the host publishes a new module-resolution generation, and hot reload expires cached package manifests.
firstReason: The goal stands: the running host follows plugin installs and removals without a restart. The mechanism is Node's module and package-configuration caches. In Go, installing or removing a plugin starts or stops a plugin process, and there is no cache to refresh.

title: Replace plugins whose loaded package files changed during profile recomposition
summary: When a profile is recomposed, plugins whose loaded package files changed on disk are evicted from Node's module cache and restarted; all recomposition goes through one exclusive path. Installing over an installed package is refused, so an upgrade is a removal followed by an install.
firstReason: Node caches a module by file URL, so an upgraded package would keep running old code. A plugin process is replaced by stopping it and starting the new binary, which removes the cause. One exclusive recomposition path is still the right shape for the Go loader.

title: Registry and Git bundle updates
summary: Third-party bundles installed from a registry or from Git can be updated from the plugins page. The host lists newer compatible versions, performs the update as remove-then-install and owns recovery if the install fails.
firstReason: The goal stands: an update path owned by the host that cannot leave the plugin uninstalled after a failure. Version listing through `pnpm view` and npm peer-dependency rules do not exist in Go; the plugin-process spec needs its own version source, compatibility check and rollback.

title: Install failures keep their diagnostics in the dialog
summary: A failed plugin installation always shows the host's diagnostic in the dialog: a silent pnpm failure streams the diagnostic the host recorded, a failed GitHub connection check streams its command line (credentials removed), output and exit status, and the failure screen keeps the settled result as well as the live stream.
firstReason: The rule (an install failure must never show an empty details pane, and the dialog and the full log agree) stands. The installer itself changes: under DH-ADR-4 there is no pnpm run, so the diagnostics come from fetching and starting a plugin process.

title: Plugin market Discover page and index reader
summary: An experimental, off-by-default bundle adds a host service that reads plugin market indexes and a Discover tab that lists their entries. Index sources are user data; the host fetches only configured URLs, refuses redirects, bounds the body and never writes the profile.
firstReason: The safe-reader rules (only configured URLs, no redirects, bounded size) carry over. What an entry installs changes under DH-ADR-4 from an npm bundle to a plugin process package, so the path from an entry to installation is redesigned.

title: Windows-lane observations wait on the state they read
summary: Two flaky Windows test cases were changed to wait for the state they assert on instead of reading it after a fixed delay, and to print a timeline when they fail.
firstReason: Upstream test maintenance: a repair of two specific test files in its suite. The lesson (a test waits on the observed state, not on the clock) is a general habit for Go tests, not a design decision.

title: Plugin-manager Git children isolate the host's command-line configuration
summary: Tests that start Git remove Git's command-line configuration variables from their environment first, so a CI host that exports them cannot change the result.
firstReason: Upstream test maintenance: a repair of two test files after a CI host leaked configuration. The lesson for Go tests that start Git is to build the child environment explicitly.

title: Limit DSH HMR to live profile configuration
summary: Proposal: keep live refresh of profile configuration, and remove replacement of running JavaScript modules; a source or framework change requires a process restart.
firstReason: Adopt: this is where the Go design already stands. Go does not load code into a running process the way Node loads a module, so code replacement becomes a restart of the plugin process (DH-ADR-4), while watching and re-applying configuration remains a loader feature.

title: Retire app-boot helpers used only by fixtures
summary: Proposal: remove two start-up helpers (an older configuration-path resolver and a single-file environment loader) that only test fixtures still call; the real launcher uses the layered environment loader and an absolute profile path.
firstReason: Adopt by omission: the Go boot package should expose one way to locate configuration and one way to load the environment, the ones the launcher uses.
